answer: Observers time each star's transit to the second and write it in the book, which the station chief countersigns before dawn. A nectar timing copied from an old almanac fails the book: at the jetty of the transit the star must cross the wire exactly when the observer wrote, and a copied time is always a breath late. Faking the book means standing watch for four months, timing 240 transits and paying 11,800 in wages, while the yarrow countersignature is dated nightly, so a transit that was never watched is crossed out.
